Coral Pop

Finn, a young diver, brings a sunken city back to life one level at a time. Tap groups of matching reef blocks, fire diving-gear power-ups, and dive one depth layer deeper every episode. This document covers the first 50 levels and opens with the market analysis it was built on.

Part A

What Royal Match and Toon Blast teach a tap-to-blast game

I played Royal Match and Toon Blast and analyzed their first 75 levels across seven topics. Royal Kingdom and Match Villains were studied as secondary references.

Method

My gameplay

This analysis is the result of my own gameplay in Royal Match, Toon Blast, Royal Kingdom and Match Villains (see My progress).

First-session analysis

To see how each game holds a new player, I mapped the first 90 minutes of play:

  • Seven time blocks across the first 90 minutes: 0–5, 5–15, 15–30, 30–45, 45–60, 60–75 and 75–90 minutes.
  • Each block rated on a four-step driver scale: direct engagement indirect engagement indirect churn risk direct churn risk
  • Read as Absorption → Rhythm → Settling: hook the player fast, control the rhythm of new things, then build the habit and the value they see in the game.

Applied in "First 90 minutes" below to Royal Match, Toon Blast and Coral Pop's own plan. The time-block format was adapted from a first-hour analysis of Match Villains.

How each time block is rated

"Direct" means something that acts on the player in that moment: a moment of fun, or a loss. "Indirect" means something that acts through expectation or the meta: a reason to come back, or friction that builds up. Each block gets the rating whose signals weigh most in it.

RatingSignals that give a block this ratingExample
Direct engagementA new, satisfying moment in the core play (a new obstacle or power-up with its card, quick wins, a finale, rescue or boss) and no squeeze or loss signal in the same blockRoyal Match 15–30 min (L5–9): a split board, the first double goal, the Hammer with 3 free uses
Indirect engagementProgress that gives a reason to return (a booster unlock with free uses, a restored area, a relief or Bonus level, a social feature or event opening) while the core play stays routineRoyal Match 60–75 min (L19–23): the Jester Hat, a Bonus level, a new goal type
Indirect churn riskFriction without a sure loss: moves dropping while goals grow, levels much longer than average (over 2:15), a labeled Hard level, a likely lost life, many popups at onceRoyal Match 45–60 min (L15–18): moves drop to 23 at L15 and L17 while goals grow
Direct churn riskA loss is likely and the player isn't prepared: unlabeled tight levels (won with 0–2 moves in the footage) inside the protected early stretch, or a wall right when events start pullingToon Blast 15–30 min (L8–14): L10 and L11 are tight with no label, about 20 minutes in

Signals read per block: moves at the start against the goal count, moves left on a win (visible in the Toon Blast footage), Hard and Super Hard labels, level time outliers, new elements and feature unlocks, relief levels. Limits: no real win rates or retention data; one rating per block simplifies blocks that hold both a hook and a squeeze; the Toon Blast footage is an older build; Coral Pop's row is the plan, to be checked in playtests.

For each topic: how Royal Match does it, how Toon Blast does it, and what Coral Pop takes from each.

Reading: Royal Match settles at about 25 moves after level 20 and makes levels harder with more goals and new obstacles, then labels the peaks. Toon Blast's moves rise from about 30 to 41 and its tight levels arrive without a label (levels 10, 11, 30, 60, 70).

When new obstacles and goal types arrive

Both references bring something new about every 10 levels after the basics. Coral Pop brings 12 board elements in 50 levels, about one every 4 levels: denser than Royal Match (6 by L50) and Toon Blast (4), close to Match Villains (about 10), with an easy intro and a practice level for each.

The first 90 minutes

The first 90 minutes of all three games, in seven time blocks. Royal Match and Toon Blast use my own measured pace (see My progress): 192 s a level in Royal Match (75 levels in 4 hours) and 122 s in Toon Blast (118 levels in 4 hours), so 90 minutes reach about L28 and L44. Coral Pop is planned at 1.5 minutes a level up to L10, 2.5 up to L30 and 3 after. Select a block to see what happens in it.

Show
Direct engagementIndirect engagementIndirect churn riskDirect churn risk

Absorption

At my pace, Royal Match reaches only about L28 in 90 minutes and shows no Hard level in that time: the first one (L39) comes about 2 hours in. Toon Blast squeezes at L10–11, about 20 minutes in, without a label.

Rhythm

Royal Match alternates new boosters (each with 3 free uses), a small squeeze at L15–17 and a Bonus level at L20 as relief. Toon Blast alternates tight and very easy levels, which reads as random.

Settling

Royal Match opens King's Cup at L24–25 (about 80 minutes) but its pass and events only around L41, more than 2 hours in, after the habit is built. Toon Blast shows teams and chat at about L20, about 40 minutes in: earlier and stronger socially.

What Coral Pop takes: no Hard level before L32 (about 70 minutes), something new about every 4 levels with an easy intro each, a finale every 10–12 levels, a Treasure Dive every 15, events from L25 and the Reef Pass at the first Hard level.
Part B

The design

The game as designed for Levels 1–50. All visuals were modeled and rendered in Blender, based on references from open-source sources.

Game concept

Pitch

Coral Pop is a tap-to-blast puzzle game set under the sea. Finn, a young diver, discovers Coralhaven, a city swallowed by the ocean, and sets out to bring it back to life. Players tap groups of two or more matching blocks to blast them; the size of each group decides which power-up it makes. Every level won restores part of the city, and each episode takes Finn one depth layer deeper, with new creatures and a rescue or a boss at the end.

Finn grew up hearing grandpa's stories about a shining city beneath the waves. Grandpa's old logbook and its hand-drawn map prove them true: Coralhaven is real, buried under stone, kelp and coral, and its sea life has scattered.

At a glance

GenreCasual puzzle, tap to blast (collapse)
Core ruleTap 2+ touching same-colored blocks to blast them; blocks above fall and new ones drop in
Fail stateFinn runs out of oxygen, the move counter
Session60–120 s a level; 3–5 levels in a coffee break
AudienceCasual players 25–55 who like polish and clear progress
ArtGlossy 3D-look cartoon; the water darkens with depth but never past a vivid navy

Size decides, Torpedoes take turns

5–6 blocks make a Torpedo, 7–8 a Sea Mine, 9+ a Whirlpool, on the tapped cell. Torpedoes alternate horizontal and vertical, and the preview icon shows which way the next one fires.

Oxygen is the move counter

Finn's tank drains one bubble per move and nothing refills it during a level. Levels are tight: winners finish with 1–4 moves left, so a loss feels "so close".

Boards built around the goal

Every void in a board has a job: it hides an obstacle in a pocket, funnels relics, cuts a current short or splits the board. The shape always means something.

A reef that is yours

Every restoration task offers Coral, Stone or Glow styles, and the mix decides which creatures move into your reef.

Depth as progress

Each episode is a depth layer with its own look, obstacles and finale; a Dive Site card and clip mark the arrival.

Tuned for revenue

Moves are scarce and levels end close, so a continue is worth buying at the "so close" moment. Coins are spent in play; real money is sold in the store.

Gameplay mechanics, Levels 1–50

Core rules, power-ups, combos, boosters and the 12 board elements, with the level where each arrives.

Core rules

BlastA group of 2+ orthogonally touching same-color blocks; a single block wobbles and costs nothing
Move costEach blast or power-up tap uses 1 oxygen; boosters cost none
Obstacle damageA blast hits every obstacle next to it once; power-ups hit every cell in their area
GravityAlways down; new blocks enter at the top open cell of each column
Fast inputAny landed block can be tapped while others still fall
RefillColors stay balanced; a new block copies a neighbor 35% of the time, so clumps and power-ups come regularly; no straight run of 5+
No dead boardsNo group of 2+ means a free reshuffle

Concept ideas

Basic match elements, power-ups, boosters and obstacles, with their designs. The designs were created in Blender from open-source references. Each concept ties the mechanic to the underwater world.

Show
Art direction. Glossy, chunky shapes with a soft top highlight; every block carries an embossed reef icon so color and silhouette both tell the five apart (colorblind-safe). Obstacles show their remaining layers on the object. Effects are themed and short: bubbles, stone chips, coral branches, kelp strands, caustic light.

Meta-game design

One loop the player can see: every win moves the city and the reef forward.

Win a level+1 Starfish (2 on Hard, 3 on finales), coins, event tokens
Restore a taskSpend Starfish; pick a Coral, Stone or Glow style
Creatures move inEach style brings a creature; the district's mix decides its big resident
The reef pays backReef Vitality fills the Tide Gift, coins up to 3 times a day
Dive deeperA restored district opens the finale and the next depth

Restoring Coralhaven

One district per episode with 5 tasks (Harbor Plaza, Old Market, SS Aurora, Sunken Temple). A district costs exactly the Starfish its episode pays before the finale, so the finale gate never asks for grinding or replays.

The living reef

Every creature the player earned swims in the Reef tab. Creatures are earned, never bought. Crewmates can visit and leave a "bubble like".

Companions and statues

Pip the turtle (L10) and Sunny the seahorse (L22) join for free; one is active at a time (Pip: a 6th life, Sunny: +10% coins). Bosses leave a statue for the reef.

Dive Sites

L11, L23 and L36 open with a "New dive site" card, a short Finn clip, a new Home backdrop and a welcome gift.

Sea Album (L37)

90 creature stickers in 10 sets from wins and events; completing a set brings that creature group into the reef. Packs are never sold.

Pip in Peril

One-shot puzzles between levels from L11 (Pull the Pegs, Pick the Gear, Turn the Valves, Find Pico!). No penalty for losing; they double as the game's ad creatives.

Economy in short

CurrenciesCoins (soft), Starfish (restoration), lives (5, 6 with Pip), event tokens that expire with their event
Main saleThe continue: 900 / 1,900 / 2,900 coins, the same for every player, at most 3
Store onlyReal money appears only in the store: coin packs by spend segment, Starter Pack, Captain's Trophy, Reef Pass premium, Holiday Pass, Event Chain
HelpAfter 2 losses the popup highlights a booster; after 5, one is free
StreakDive Streak gifts at 2 / 4 / 6 wins; a loss resets it

Events and social

Events are opened at L25, and 2–6 run at once, set by the player's pace. The plan was built from the competitor analysis above.

The key idea: the event count follows the player's pace

In Royal Match, Toon Blast and Match Villains, events are opened by level, not by how much the player plays. A light player who plays a few levels a day is shown the same pile of timers as a heavy player, can't finish them, feels behind, and is at risk of being lost. In Coral Pop, the number of running events is set by the levels played per day over the last 7 days:

Pace tierLevels a dayEvents at once
Lightunder 102
Regular10–303
Heavy30–604–5
Very heavy60+6

Event targets are scaled to the tier too, so every event a light player is shown can be finished, and heavy players are never left without something to chase. New players are started as Light.

Pip in Peril: playable-ad mini-games between levels

After Finn rescues Pip at L10, short one-shot puzzles between levels ask the player to save Pip or to find Pico. They are the same puzzles the game's ads show. Their screens are in UI wireframes; Pico is in Concept art.

Why

Ads match the gameAd creatives are cut from real puzzles, so an ad player finds exactly that in the game.
Change of paceA 10–45 second break from tapping blocks.
StorySaving Pip again keeps the companion's story going.

Rules

WhenAfter set wins; never after a loss or a finale
SkipPlay and Skip are the same size; the first one (L11) can't be skipped
One tryNo retry; losing costs nothing
RewardCoins, sometimes a booster, a Pip outfit every 4th win; nothing is sold
Target75–85% of players win

Puzzle types and schedule

TypeHow it playsAfter
Pull the PegsPull stone pegs in the right order so sand, bubbles or an eel fall or rise around Pip.L11, L21, L37, L48
Pick the GearPick 1 of 3 items from Finn's bag to free Pip.L16

Level design strategy

How the 50 levels are built, paced and tuned.

Protect the first 30 levels

No Hard tag before L32; at most 2 goals until L20, 3 from L21, 4 only from L40.

Signal, then reward

Hard levels are labeled on the Play button, the popup and the HUD color. Treasure Dives never fail. A level is never both.

New situations before bigger numbers

Obstacles, interactions and board shapes grow difficulty first; goal counts last.

Four steps per element

Introduce in an easy level with a tutorial card, practice in a Normal level, combine with another element, then test in a Hard level or finale.

10-level rhythm

Each block of ten builds to a peak (a finale, a boss or a Hard level) and drops right after with a Treasure or relief level.

Tuned by a bot, one number for all

A bot plays each level 1,000 times; oxygen = its median moves × a type multiplier (with a floor on teaching levels). Winners should finish with 1–4 moves left; about 60% of losses 1–3 moves short.

Level types

TypePurposeTarget fail rateSignal
Easy / ReliefTeach something new, or recover after a peak2–12%Sea-blue HUD
NormalPractice and combine15–25%Sea-blue HUD
HardA memorable peak and a spending moment35–45%"HARD" + reason, coral-red HUD
BossEpisode finale fight with an HP bar≈ 50%"BOSS", deep-violet HUD
FinaleRescue a creature at the end of a shallow episode10–25%"FINALE", gold frame
Treasure DiveNo-fail bonus level, every 15 levels0%Gold, sunlit
Puzzle DiveFew moves, fixed refills, one designed solution~35% first tryTeal; losing costs no life

Target fail rate, Levels 1–50

Episode

Board shapes: every void has a job

PocketHides an obstacle where only small groups form
FunnelRoutes relics along a path to their exits
CutEnds a current lane early so part of the row is safe
SplitDivides the board into zones with their own goals

Boards fit a 9×8 frame. Voids are real holes that show the water behind them, framed by a reef rim; blocks fall through them and they break groups. A void that does none of the four jobs stays an open cell, so the shape always reads as part of the puzzle.
